newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson's civil case in the hands of the jury.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson's civil case in the hands of the jury.

text.p: The jury in the O.J. Simpson civil case began deliberations on Tuesday after being told by the judge to ignore the former football star's acquittal in 1995 of murdering his ex-wife and her friend.
There was a heavy police presence around the courtroom as Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki gave his instructions to the predominantly white panel, ending three months of dramatic testimony from both sides.

The seven-woman, five-man panel began deliberating after hearing a last emotional plea from the plaintiffs' lead attorney asking them to find Simpson responsible for the murders of his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.
The jury, which is not sequestered, deliberated for about 90 minutes before adjourning for the day and was to resume on Wednesday morning.

Fujisaki directed the panel -- consisting of nine whites, one Asian-black, one Hispanic and one black -- to disregard Simpson's acquittal by a mostly black criminal court jury in October 1995 and to ignore a recent family court ruling that gave Simpson custody of his two young children by his ex-wife.

Unlike a criminal trial, the jury verdict does not have to be unanimous and may be decided by a 9-3 majority. Also it only has to find on the basis of a "preponderance of evidence" rather than "beyond a reasonable doubt."
Simpson, a former TV personality, actor and pitchman, is being sued by the victims' families in a wrongful death action.

If found responsible for the deaths, he could be forced to pay millions of dollars in damages, but recent reports say his wealth has dwindled since the criminal trial and his fortune is now estimated at around $3 million.

Specifically, the jurors are being asked first to find if they believe Simpson is responsible for the death of Goldman. In a separate question they must decide if he is responsible for the "battery" against his ex-wife that caused her death.
Technically, her estate's claim is a "survivorship" suit and is not for "wrongful death," which an estate cannot sue for under California law.

In the event the jury finds Simpson responsible, the panel must also give the amount of compensatory damages they are awarding Goldman's father, Fred, and his natural mother, Sharon Rufo, for their loss of "love, companionship, affection and support."
Next would follow the punitive damages phase in which the jury would be asked to punish Simpson for his actions by imposing further damages.

In his rebuttal of defence closing arguments, Daniel Petrocelli, who represents Fred Goldman, said the low point of the trial came on Monday as Simpson's attorney Robert Baker "mocked" the victims' families when he told the jury the case was about money and that it only cost $200 to file a suit in California.

Brandishing $200 in bills, he marched across the courtroom to a seated Simpson and shouted: "You know, Mr Simpson? Here's $200, you want it? Give my client back his son and we will march out of here in a heartbeat."
Describing Simpson's stormy relationship with his ex-wife, Petrocelli said: "They had been at war with each other and she's found dead. Coincidence?"

He told jurors not to be concerned about Simpson's motive for the crime, saying: "People, sadly, have been killed in relationships from day one. Revenge, love, hatred and jealousy - the oldest things known to man."

Deriding Simpson's claim that he had never struck his former wife, Petrocelli accused Simpson of "audacity" for making such a statement during his testimony when the jury had been shown a photograph of a bruised and battered Nicole Brown Simpson.
"Mothers of children get killed all the time, men beat mothers of children, men kill mothers of children," he said.

In testimony and closing arguments, Simpson's attorneys tried to show that evidence in the case was planted, that it was contaminated by sloppy laboratory work and that the police bungled their investigation.
